# Google Rust Style Guide

> **Source:** [Google Rust Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/rustguide.html)
>
> Google's own Rust rules. Binding for library code; strong recommendation for application code. Overrides the Rust Style Guide and API Guidelines on conflict.

## [Background and Scope](01-background-and-scope.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-BG-01](01-background-and-scope.md#g-bg-01) | Follow public Rust style rules | Code **MUST** follow the official public Rust style rules to the extent they don't conflict with this style guide. |
| [G-BG-02](01-background-and-scope.md#g-bg-02) | Apply API design rules in context | When applying API design rules, distinguish library code from application code. For library code, API design rules are binding (**MUST**); for application code, they are a strong recommendation (**SHOULD**). |

## [Code Organization](02-code-organization.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-ORG-01](02-code-organization.md#g-org-01) | Prefer small crates `[chrome]` | Crates **SHOULD** be small; ideally, but not necessarily, a single file focusing on one abstraction. If code can be split into small crates, it **SHOULD** be. *Applies to: `[chrome]` Chromium only.* |
| [G-ORG-02](02-code-organization.md#g-org-02) | Use flat file layout for `rust_library` sources `[chrome]` | All `.rs` source files of one `rust_library` (one Rust crate) **MUST** reside in a single directory. Subdirectories **MUST NOT** be used to organize files belonging to a single crate. *Applies to: `[chrome]` Chromium only.* |
| [G-ORG-03](02-code-organization.md#g-org-03) | Name source files and leaf modules after the primary user-defined item | When a leaf module has a primary user-defined item (e.g., `Foo`), the module **SHOULD** be named after that item (e.g., `mod foo` and `foo.rs`). |
| [G-ORG-04](02-code-organization.md#g-org-04) | Don't implement APIs in non-leaf modules | Non-leaf modules **SHOULD** contain only module declarations (not definitions) and re-exports. |
| [G-ORG-05](02-code-organization.md#g-org-05) | Don't use glob imports | Code **MUST NOT** use glob imports (`use path::*`), except in the cases listed below, where you **MAY** use them at your own discretion. |
| [G-ORG-06](02-code-organization.md#g-org-06) | A `use` statement should import items from one module | Each `use` statement **SHOULD** import items from a single module: there should be no `::` inside the `{..}` block of a `use` statement. |
| [G-ORG-07](02-code-organization.md#g-org-07) | Prefer locally-scoped trait imports | Traits **SHOULD** be imported within function bodies, unless the trait's methods are used extensively throughout the file. |
| [G-ORG-08](02-code-organization.md#g-org-08) | Qualify calls to top-level functions with a module name | To use top-level functions defined in other modules or crates, you **MUST** import their module and call them as `modulename::functionname()`. |
| [G-ORG-09](02-code-organization.md#g-org-09) | Type names should be imported and used unqualified | By default, types and traits **SHOULD** be referenced without their module path (e.g., `Regex`, not `regex::Regex`), with a `use regex::Regex` at the top of the file or potentially in the relevant function. |
| [G-ORG-10](02-code-organization.md#g-org-10) | Use the appropriate import mechanism `[chrome]` | In Chromium, code **MUST** use `chromium::import!()` as the import mechanism. *Applies to: `[chrome]` Chromium only.* |

## [Code Formatting and Aesthetics](03-formatting.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-FMT-01](03-formatting.md#g-fmt-01) | Use the appropriate formatting tool | Code **MUST** be formatted with the codebase's appropriate formatting tool (e.g., `git cl format` in Chromium). |
| [G-FMT-02](03-formatting.md#g-fmt-02) | Opting out of automatic formatting | You **MAY** opt out of automatic formatting with `#[rustfmt::skip]`, but only in the situations listed below. Formatting **SHOULD NOT** be skipped for personal style choices. |

## [Ownership and borrowing](04-ownership-and-borrowing.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-OWN-01](04-ownership-and-borrowing.md#g-own-01) | Avoid `Rc` and `Arc` | You **SHOULD** prefer unique ownership and borrowing over `Rc` and `Arc` for managing memory. |
| [G-OWN-02](04-ownership-and-borrowing.md#g-own-02) | Prefer borrows over deep copies | Use `.clone()` when you genuinely need a deep copy of an object. You **SHOULD NOT** use `.clone()` as a substitute for borrowing; design code that works naturally with Rust's ownership and borrowing rules. |

## [Function inputs and outputs](05-function-inputs-and-outputs.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-FIO-01](05-function-inputs-and-outputs.md#g-fio-01) | Accept flexible references for immutable data | When a function accepts borrowed, immutable data, it **MUST** use the reference type that affords the most flexibility: pass references to the data itself, not references to smart pointers, containers, or wrappers. |
| [G-FIO-02](05-function-inputs-and-outputs.md#g-fio-02) | Iterators vs. owned collections in return types | You **SHOULD** prefer returning iterators (either concrete types or `impl Iterator`) over returning `Vec<T>` where possible. |
| [G-FIO-03](05-function-inputs-and-outputs.md#g-fio-03) | Iterators vs. slices in function parameters | Highly reusable library code **SHOULD** accept iterators or `impl IntoIterator` if it only needs to iterate over the input. *Applies to: highly reusable library code.* |
| [G-FIO-04](05-function-inputs-and-outputs.md#g-fio-04) | Accepting `Into` | When designing library APIs that accept a `T` but users are likely to have various types, you **SHOULD** consider accepting `impl Into<T>` instead of `T` if **call-site ergonomics are paramount**. *Applies to: library APIs.* |
| [G-FIO-05](05-function-inputs-and-outputs.md#g-fio-05) | Prefer `enum` over `bool` in APIs | You **SHOULD** use `enum` function parameters instead of `bool` where the purpose of the parameter is not obvious. |
| [G-FIO-06](05-function-inputs-and-outputs.md#g-fio-06) | Reporting errors | You **MUST** choose the error reporting mechanism that fits your API contract: `Option`, `Result`, or `panic!`. |

## [Types](06-types.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-TYP-01](06-types.md#g-typ-01) | Newtypes versus type aliases | You **MUST** use a [newtype](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/generics/new_types.html) instead of a type alias in the cases listed below. |
| [G-TYP-02](06-types.md#g-typ-02) | Prefer named fields over tuples and non-newtype tuple structs | You **SHOULD** prefer types with named fields over tuples, as tuple indexes (`.0`, `.1`, ...) quickly become confusing. |

## [Traits](07-traits.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-TRT-01](07-traits.md#g-trt-01) | Add trait implementations when they become necessary | As a general rule, low-level library code **SHOULD** anticipate users' needs proactively, while application code **SHOULD** add trait impls as needed. |
| [G-TRT-02](07-traits.md#g-trt-02) | Implement known standard library traits instead of custom methods | If a method matches the purpose and behavior of a standard library trait, you **SHOULD** implement that trait (e.g. `impl FromStr for Foo` instead of `fn from_str(&str) -> Self` on `Foo`). |
| [G-TRT-03](07-traits.md#g-trt-03) | Use `#[derive()]` if possible | Manual trait implementations **SHOULD NOT** be written if they can be expressed as a `#[derive()]`. |
| [G-TRT-04](07-traits.md#g-trt-04) | Generics versus `dyn Trait` | In libraries, function parameters **SHOULD** accept generics (`T: Trait` or `impl Trait`) rather than `dyn Trait`. *Applies to: library code.* |
| [G-TRT-05](07-traits.md#g-trt-05) | When to define a trait versus an inherent implementation | You **MUST** define a trait only for the purposes listed below; in all other cases where you want to implement functionality for a type, use an [inherent implementation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/keyword.impl.html#inherent-implementations). You **MUST NOT** use traits merely to organize code. |
| [G-TRT-06](07-traits.md#g-trt-06) | Extension traits | An extension trait's name **SHOULD** carry the suffix `~Ext` (e.g. `ForeignTypeExt`). In general, the team that owns the original type **SHOULD** also own the extension trait. |
| [G-TRT-07](07-traits.md#g-trt-07) | Specific guidance for important traits | Important standard traits are implemented according to the per-trait guidance below; the requirement strength is marked on each item. |
| [G-TRT-08](07-traits.md#g-trt-08) | Pair important `From` impls with explicit constructor methods | If a type has an important `From` impl expected to be one of the primary ways of constructing it, you **MUST** also add an inherent `::new()`, `::new_from_foo()`, or `::from_foo()` method. |
| [G-TRT-09](07-traits.md#g-trt-09) | Options structs should implement Default | Structs with all-public fields that are primarily used as a "bag of options" for a function **SHOULD** implement `Default`. |

## [Concurrency](08-concurrency.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-CON-01](08-concurrency.md#g-con-01) | Handling poison | You **MUST NOT** reach inside a poisoned mutex to get at its insides, no matter how tempting the use case may seem. |
| [G-CON-02](08-concurrency.md#g-con-02) | Don't use `async` / `.await` `[chrome]` | You **MUST NOT** use `async` / `.await` in Chromium. *Applies to: `[chrome]` Chromium only.* |
| [G-CON-03](08-concurrency.md#g-con-03) | Don't start new threads through the Rust standard library `[chrome]` | You **SHOULD NOT** start new threads through the Rust standard library in Chromium; prefer sequences instead of threads. *Applies to: `[chrome]` Chromium only.* |
| [G-CON-04](08-concurrency.md#g-con-04) | Use `fuchsia_sync::Mutex` `[Fuchsia]` | You **MUST** use Fuchsia's mutex type (`fuchsia_sync::Mutex`) rather than one from `std::sync` or `parking_lot`. *Applies to: `[Fuchsia]` Fuchsia only.* |

## [Macros](09-macros.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-MAC-01](09-macros.md#g-mac-01) | Prefer non-macro facilities, in order | When considering how to express an API, you **SHOULD** prefer, in order: 1. Regular Rust functions, types, traits, objects, and modules (avoid macros, code generation, and metaprogramming where possible). 2. `macro_rules!`-style macros. 3. Other code generation strategies (e.g. `genrule`). 4. `proc_macro` macros. |
| [G-MAC-02](09-macros.md#g-mac-02) | Weigh the costs of macros and code generation | When you decide to use a macro or code generation, you **SHOULD** weigh the benefits against the costs. |

## [Naming](10-naming.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-NAM-01](10-naming.md#g-nam-01) | Naming methods | Method names **MUST** follow the Rust standard library style. Methods **MUST** use prefixes such as `as_...()`, `to_...()` or `into_...()` with the appropriate `self` convention. |
| [G-NAM-02](10-naming.md#g-nam-02) | Naming lifetimes | Lifetimes **SHOULD** have descriptive names, especially type lifetimes. |
| [G-NAM-03](10-naming.md#g-nam-03) | Naming generic parameters | Generic parameters **MUST** have a short name (single or multi character) related to the kind of thing they represent. |
| [G-NAM-04](10-naming.md#g-nam-04) | Naming extension traits | An [extension trait](07-traits.md#g-trt-06) name **MUST** have an `~Ext` suffix (for example, `ForeignTypeExt`). |
| [G-NAM-05](10-naming.md#g-nam-05) | Naming initialization functions | Initialization functions **MUST** follow these naming conventions. |
| [G-NAM-06](10-naming.md#g-nam-06) | Avoid abbreviations | Names **MUST NOT** use abbreviations (especially acronyms and initialisms) that someone outside your project is unlikely to know, and **MUST NOT** abbreviate by deleting letters within a word. |

## [When and how to write documentation](11-documentation.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-DOC-01](11-documentation.md#g-doc-01) | Document public APIs | Public APIs **MUST** have documentation comments; the `missing_docs` lint **MAY** be used to help enforce this. |
| [G-DOC-02](11-documentation.md#g-doc-02) | Consider including examples | Documentation **SHOULD** include examples: not every function needs one, but enough functionality **SHOULD** be covered by examples *somewhere* to give an idea of how the crate works. |
| [G-DOC-03](11-documentation.md#g-doc-03) | Document panic cases | Functions that may panic due to malformed input **MUST** always document their panic cases. |
| [G-DOC-04](11-documentation.md#g-doc-04) | Document invariants of unsafe functions and traits | Unsafe functions and traits **MUST** clearly document their invariants. |
| [G-DOC-05](11-documentation.md#g-doc-05) | Use capitalization and punctuation | Documentation comments **MUST** use capitalization and punctuation. |
| [G-DOC-06](11-documentation.md#g-doc-06) | Don't explain language basics | Documentation **MUST NOT** explain the basics of the programming language. |
| [G-DOC-07](11-documentation.md#g-doc-07) | Use `///` for item documentation | Items following the comment, such as functions, structs, enums, traits and type aliases, **MUST** be documented with `///` comments. |
| [G-DOC-08](11-documentation.md#g-doc-08) | Use `//!` for module and library documentation | The module or library itself **MUST** be documented with `//!` comments, which **SHOULD** be placed at the top of the file. |
| [G-DOC-09](11-documentation.md#g-doc-09) | Follow the Rust style guide's doc-comment rules | Doc comments **MUST** follow the rules in the official Rust style guide on doc comments. |
| [G-DOC-10](11-documentation.md#g-doc-10) | Use Markdown syntax | Doc comments **MUST** use Markdown syntax. |
| [G-DOC-11](11-documentation.md#g-doc-11) | Use `//` for non-documentation comments | Non-documentation comments (implementation comments, TODOs not interesting to users, commented-out source code, etc.) **MUST** use ordinary `//` comment syntax. |
| [G-DOC-12](11-documentation.md#g-doc-12) | Prefer direct doc comments over macro-generated docs | Documentation **SHOULD** be written directly with `///` and `//!` comments rather than generated from macros. |

## [Other Rust features](12-other-rust-features.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-FEAT-01](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-01) | Unsafe code | **MUST NOT** write unsafe code unless there is no way to implement the same functionality with safe code. |
| [G-FEAT-02](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-02) | No unstable features | **MUST NOT** use unstable features. |
| [G-FEAT-03](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-03) | Getters and setters | Writing and naming getters and setters **SHOULD** follow the naming guidelines below. |
| [G-FEAT-04](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-04) | Implement expected API sets together | If you implement `len()`, you **MUST** also implement `is_empty()`. |
| [G-FEAT-05](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-05) | Don't access `#[doc(hidden)]` items you don't own | Treat items marked `#[doc(hidden)]` as private: you **MUST NOT** access them unless you own the code. |
| [G-FEAT-06](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-06) | Use `const` functions responsibly | **MUST NOT** mark a public function `const` unless you expect it to remain `const` in the future (or can commit to helping clients migrate when it changes). |
| [G-FEAT-07](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-07) | Avoid overloading for non-mathematical purposes | Use operator overloads for their original mathematical/logical purpose; **SHOULD NOT** use them merely to make code more concise ("syntax sugar"). |
| [G-FEAT-08](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-08) | `#[non_exhaustive]` on publicly-exposed enums | If an enum is part of a public API used by other teams, you **MUST** mark it `#[non_exhaustive]`. *Applies to: Public APIs used by other teams.* |
| [G-FEAT-09](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-09) | `#[non_exhaustive]` on public structs with public fields | Structs with public fields that are part of a public API used by other teams **SHOULD** be marked `#[non_exhaustive]`. *Applies to: Public APIs used by other teams.* |
| [G-FEAT-10](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-10) | `#[must_use]` on functions | You **MUST** use `#[must_use]` on functions in the cases below. |
| [G-FEAT-11](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-11) | `#[must_use]` on types | You **MUST** use `#[must_use]` on types intended to be returned by functions that would otherwise be annotated `#[must_use]` per [G-FEAT-10](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-10). |
| [G-FEAT-12](12-other-rust-features.md#g-feat-12) | Don't run code before `main()` | **MUST NOT** cause code to run before `main()`, e.g. via techniques such as the [ctor crate](https://docs.rs/ctor/latest/ctor/). |

## [Implementation concerns](13-implementation-concerns.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-IMPL-01](13-implementation-concerns.md#g-impl-01) | Don't overuse type inference | You **MUST** add enough explicit types so that someone familiar with the codebase can figure out what the inferred types are. |
| [G-IMPL-02](13-implementation-concerns.md#g-impl-02) | Prefer pattern matching over check-then-unwrap | **SHOULD NOT** use potentially panicking operations when the input data guarantees they cannot panic; use pattern matching to prove correctness to the compiler instead (e.g. instead of `Option::unwrap` on a value known to be valid). |
| [G-IMPL-03](13-implementation-concerns.md#g-impl-03) | Prefer `expect` over `unwrap` | If a panic is necessary because an invariant cannot be expressed in the type system, **SHOULD** use `expect` rather than `unwrap` to document the reason. |
| [G-IMPL-04](13-implementation-concerns.md#g-impl-04) | Don't omit patterns on `non_exhaustive` enums when matching | When matching on a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum, **SHOULD** list all its variants in `match` statements. |
| [G-IMPL-05](13-implementation-concerns.md#g-impl-05) | Use context strings to clarify assertions | **SHOULD** always consider passing the optional format-string argument to `assert!` to explain why the assertion is expected to hold or what caused its violation. |
| [G-IMPL-06](13-implementation-concerns.md#g-impl-06) | Don't use iterator combinator chains when direct iteration is clearer | **SHOULD NOT** use combinator chains in ways that hurt readability. |
| [G-IMPL-07](13-implementation-concerns.md#g-impl-07) | Don't call `panic::catch_unwind` | Use of `panic::catch_unwind` is prohibited (**MUST NOT**) in first-party Rust code. |
| [G-IMPL-08](13-implementation-concerns.md#g-impl-08) | Prefer `format!` / `write!` for concatenation and substitution | **SHOULD** use `format!()` and `write!()` rather than alternatives when concatenating more than two strings or substituting into a literal string. |

## [Testing](14-testing.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [G-TEST-01](14-testing.md#g-test-01) | Use the right per-codebase test framework | **MUST** use your codebase's specific test framework; most codebases use their own rather than plain `#[test]`. |
